drills.q: Name the three families of feature selection in one line each.
drills.a: Filter: score feature vs target, no model, cheap, misses interactions. Wrapper: use real model performance as the score (RFE), expensive, most accurate. Embedded: selection is a byproduct of training one model (L1, tree importance), cheap and interaction-aware but inherits model bias.

drills.q: Your colleague fits SelectKBest(k=20) on the full dataset, then does train_test_split, then reports a 0.90 CV AUC. What's wrong?
drills.a: Selection leakage -- the top-20 features were partly chosen using label information from rows now in the test set, inflating the reported score. Selection must be inside a Pipeline, refit per CV fold.

drills.q: A random forest's feature_importances_ ranks a 50,000-category zip+4 column as the #1 feature, above a domain-known strong predictor. What do you suspect, and what do you check with instead?
drills.a: Gini/MDI cardinality bias -- more candidate split thresholds on the high-cardinality column produce spuriously good-looking splits (Strobl et al. 2007). Re-check with permutation importance or SHAP on held-out data.

drills.q: You have y = X1 XOR X2 in your data, plus 50 other genuinely irrelevant features. You run a chi2 filter and keep the top 10. What happens to X1 and X2, and why?
drills.a: Both get dropped. Filter methods score each feature marginally against y; X1 and X2 are each individually uncorrelated with y by construction of XOR, so chi2 sees no signal in either, regardless of the joint relationship.

drills.q: Design a permutation-importance check that would catch the failure mode where two highly correlated features both score as 'unimportant' despite the pair mattering.
drills.a: Cluster features by correlation (hierarchical clustering on 1 - |corr|) before running permutation importance, then compare within-cluster importance sums against between-cluster importance, rather than trusting individual per-feature scores -- shuffling one of a correlated pair barely hurts the score since the model still has the redundant other one.

drills.q: You're selecting features via L1 logistic regression and one feature is measured in the thousands (revenue) while others are 0-1 flags. Selection keeps revenue and drops flags that domain knowledge says matter. Diagnose.
drills.a: L1 penalty acts on raw coefficient magnitude, and it wasn't scaled -- revenue's larger raw scale means a smaller coefficient achieves the same predictive contribution, so it's penalized less per unit of value than the properly-scaled flags. Fix: scale all features before L1, since the penalty is scale-dependent.

drills.q: You need to run RFECV on 400 features with a 500-tree gradient boosted model and 5-fold CV, but only have a 2-hour compute budget. What do you change and what do you give up?
drills.a: Increase step from 1 to something like 0.1 (drop 10% of remaining features per round) or switch to embedded selection (native gain importance, CV-validated threshold, trains once). Tradeoff: coarser stepping evaluates and drops features in batches, so a borderline feature might get cut alongside genuinely weak ones -- an explicit accuracy-for-speed tradeoff.

drills.q: Design the feature selection stage of a fraud model with 10,000 candidate features, a 3-week deadline, and a hard requirement that a regulator can audit which features drove decisions. Outline the pipeline.
drills.a: Stage it: filter (variance threshold + mutual information) cuts 10,000 to a few hundred plus manual removal of identifiers/leakage candidates; embedded selection (gradient boosted tree gain importance, CV-validated threshold) cuts to 30-60; SHAP on the final model provides both accuracy insight and audit documentation via its local-accuracy and consistency guarantees. Every step lives inside the CV loop; final feature list is pinned and versioned, not recomputed at serve time.

drills.q: Explain the curse of dimensionality with a concrete number, and state which model families are most vs least affected.
drills.a: Matching the sample density of N points in 1D requires N^d points in d dimensions -- N=100, d=10 needs 10^20 points. Distance/density-based methods (kNN, LOF, kernel SVMs) are hit hardest since they depend on meaningful distances; tree ensembles degrade more gracefully since they partition axis-by-axis.

drills.q: You add 200 new features to a fraud model. Offline AUC improves by 0.03 but the online A/B test shows zero lift. Give your top two hypotheses in order.
drills.a: 1) Training-serving skew in the new features specifically -- offline features often use info not actually available or correctly computed online (stale batch aggregate, or a feature with a downstream-event leak). 2) The 0.03 offline lift itself leaked through feature selection or tuning done on the same data used to report it. Check feature parity between training and serving before doubting the online experiment's power.

drills.q: Why might explicit feature selection provide zero accuracy benefit on a well-tuned XGBoost model with reg_alpha/reg_lambda and min_child_weight set, and could it ever hurt?
drills.a: Regularized gradient boosted trees are already fairly robust to irrelevant features, so selection mainly buys latency and interpretability rather than accuracy. It can actively hurt if it drops a feature that only carries signal in combination with another (an XOR-style interaction), since single-feature importance scores can't see that.
